entries.3cade74643ba9fad76ba0cd4e17f84cafd2e8049: <div sID="gen9943" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Job.29" sID="Job.29"/> <div eID="gen9943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9944" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9945" type="x-p"/> After that excellent discourse concerning wisdom in the foregoing chapter Job sat down and paused awhile, not because he had talked himself out of breath, but because he would not, without the leave of the company, engross the talk to himself, but would give room for his friends, if they pleased, to make their remarks on what he had said; but they had nothing to say, and therefore, after he had recollected himself a little, he went on with his discourse concerning his own affairs, as recorded in this and the two following chapters, in which, I. He describes the height of the prosperity from which he had fallen. And, II. The depth of the adversity into which he had fallen; and this he does to move the pity of his friends, and to justify, or at least excuse, his own complaints. But then, III. To obviate his friends' censures of him, he makes a very ample and particular protestation of his own integrity notwithstanding. In this chapter he looks back to the days of his prosperity, and shows, 1. What comfort and satisfaction he had in his house and family, <reference osisRef="Job.29.1-Job.29.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. 2. What a great deal of honour and power he had in his country, and what respect was paid him by all sorts of people, <reference osisRef="Job.29.7-Job.29.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. 3. What abundance of good he did in his place, as a magistrate, <reference osisRef="Job.29.11-Job.29.17">ver. 11-17</reference>. 4. What a just prospect he had of the continuance of his comfort at home (<reference osisRef="Job.29.18-Job.29.20">ver. 18-20</reference>) and of his interest abroad, <reference osisRef="Job.29.21-Job.29.25">ver. 21-25</reference>. All this he enlarges upon, to aggravate his present calamities; like Naomi, "I went out full," but am brought "home again empty."
entries.3b4a7c44cedc8ca461ef1acb6afc640a9321b4a7: <div eID="gen9945" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9944" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Former Prosperity of Job. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9946" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 Oh that I were as <hi type="italic">in</hi> months past, as <hi type="italic">in</hi> the days <hi type="italic">when</hi> God preserved me; <hi type="super">3</hi> When his candle shined upon my head, <hi type="italic">and when</hi> by his light I walked <hi type="italic">through</hi> darkness; <hi type="super">4</hi> As I was in the days of my youth, when the secret of God <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon my tabernacle; <hi type="super">5</hi> When the Almighty <hi type="italic">was</hi> yet with me, <hi type="italic">when</hi> my children <hi type="italic">were</hi> about me; <hi type="super">6</hi> When I washed my steps with butter, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil; <div eID="gen9946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9947" type="x-p"/> Losers may have leave to speak, and there is nothing they speak of more feelingly than of the comforts they are stripped of. Their former prosperity is one of the most pleasing subjects of their thoughts and talk. It was so to Job, who begins here with a wish (<reference osisRef="Job.29.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">O that I were as in months past!</hi> so he brings in this account of his prosperity. His wish is, 1. "O that I were in as good a state as I was in then, that I had as much wealth, honour, and pleasure, as I had then!" This he wishes, from a concern he had, not so much for his ease, as for his reputation and the glory of his God, which he thought were eclipsed by his present sufferings. "O that I might be restored to my prosperity, and then the censures and reproaches of my friends would be effectually silenced, even upon their own principles, and for ever rolled away!" If this be our end in desiring life, health, and prosperity, that God may be glorified, and the credit of our holy profession rescued, preserved, and advanced, the desire is not only natural, but spiritual. 2. "O that I were in as good a frame of spirit as I was in then!" That which Job complained most of now was a load upon his spirits, through God's withdrawing from him; and therefore he wishes he now had his spirit as much enlarged and encouraged in the service of God as he had then and that he had as much freedom and fellowship with him as then thought himself happy in. This was <hi type="italic">in the days of his youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.29.4">v. 4</reference>), when he was in the prime of his time for the enjoyment of those things and could relish them with the highest gust. Note, Those that prosper in the days of their youth know not what black and cloudy days they are yet reserved for. Two things made the months past pleasant to Job:— <div eID="gen9947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9948" type="x-p"/> I. That he had comfort in his God. This was the chief thing he rejoiced in, in his prosperity, as the spring of it and the sweetness of it, that he had the favour of God and the tokens of that favour. He did not attribute his prosperity to a happy turn of fortune, nor to his own might, nor to the power of his own hand, but makes the same acknowledgment that David does. <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Ps. xxx. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou, by thy favour, hast made my mountain stand strong.</hi> A gracious soul delights in God's smiles, not in the smiles of this world. Four things were then very pleasant to holy Job:—1. The confidence he had in the divine protection. They were <hi type="italic">the days when God preserved me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.29.2">v. 2</reference>. Even then he saw himself exposed, and did not make <hi type="italic">his wealth his strong city</hi> nor <hi type="italic">trust in the abundance of his riches,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the name of the Lord was his strong tower;</hi> in that only he thought himself safe, and to that he ascribed it that he was then safe and that his comforts were preserved to him. The devil saw a hedge about him of God's making (<reference osisRef="Job.1.10">ch. i. 10</reference>), and Job saw it himself, and owned it was <hi type="italic">God's visitation that preserved his spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.12">ch. x. 12</reference>. Those only whom God protects are safe and may be easy; and therefore those who have ever so much of this world must not think themselves safe unless God preserve them. 2. The complacency he had in the divine favour (<reference osisRef="Job.29.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">God's candle shone upon his head,</hi> that is, God lifted up the light of his countenance upon him, gave him the assurances and sweet relishes of his love. The best of the communications of the divine favour to the saints in this world is but the candle-light, compared with what is reserved for them in the future state. But such abundant satisfaction did Job take in the divine favour that, by the light of that, he walked through darkness; that guided him in his doubts, comforted him in his griefs, bore him up under his burdens, and helped him through all his difficulties. Those that have the brightest sun-shine of outward prosperity must yet expect some moments of darkness. They are sometimes crossed, sometimes at a loss, sometimes melancholy. But those that are interested in the favour of God, and know how to value it, can, by the light of that, walk cheerfully and comfortably through all the darkness of this vale of tears. That puts gladness into the heart enough to counterbalance all the grievances of this present time. 3. The communion he had with the divine word (<reference osisRef="Job.29.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The secret of God was upon my tabernacle,</hi> that is, God conversed freely with him, as one bosom-friend with another. He knew God's mind, and was not in the dark about it, as, of late, he had been. <hi type="italic">The secret of the Lord is</hi> said to be <hi type="italic">with those that fear him,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he shows them</hi> that in <hi type="italic">his covenant</hi> which others see not, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>. God communicates his favour and grace to his people, and receives the return of their devotion in a way secret to the world. Some read it, <hi type="italic">When the society of God was in my tabernacle,</hi> which Rabbi Solomon understands of an assembly of God's people that used to meet at Job's house for religious worship, in which he presided; this he took a great deal of pleasure in, and the scattering of it was a trouble to him. Or it may be understood of the angels of God pitching their tents about his habitation. 4. The assurance he had of the divine presence (<reference osisRef="Job.29.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Almighty was yet with me.</hi> Now he thought God had departed from him, but in those days he was <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> and that was all in all to him. God's presence with a man in his house, though it be but a cottage, makes it both a castle and a palace. <div eID="gen9948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9949" type="x-p"/> II. That he had comfort in his family. Every thing was agreeable there: he had both mouths for his meat and meat for his mouths; the want of either is a great affliction. 1. He had a numerous offspring to enjoy his estate: <hi type="italic">My children were about me.</hi> He had many children, enough to compass him round, and they were observant of him and obsequious to him; they were about him, to know what he would have and wherein they might serve him. It is a comfort to tender parents to see their children about them. Job speaks very feelingly of this comfort now that he was deprived of it. He thought it an instance of God's being with him that his children were about him; and yet reckon amiss if, when we have lost our children, we cannot comfort ourselves with this, that we have not lost our God. 2. He had a plentiful estate for the support of this numerous family, <reference osisRef="Job.29.6">v. 6</reference>. His dairy abounded to such a degree that he might, if he pleased, <hi type="italic">wash his steps with butter;</hi> and his olive-yards were so fruitful, beyond expectation, that it seemed as if the <hi type="italic">rock poured him out rivers of oil.</hi> He reckons his wealth, not by his silver and gold, which were for hoarding, but by his butter and oil, which were for use; for what is an estate good for unless we take the good of it ourselves and do good with it to others?
entries.77f19b14165c3a51af0f749ab784c08e6292a7c4: <div eID="gen9949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> When I went out to the gate through the city, <hi type="italic">when</hi> I prepared my seat in the street! <hi type="super">8</hi> The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, <hi type="italic">and</hi> stood up. <hi type="super">9</hi> The princes refrained talking, and laid <hi type="italic">their</hi> hand on their mouth. <hi type="super">10</hi> The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth. <hi type="super">11</hi> When the ear heard <hi type="italic">me,</hi> then it blessed me; and when the eye saw <hi type="italic">me,</hi> it gave witness to me: <hi type="super">12</hi> Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and <hi type="italic">him that had</hi> none to help him. <hi type="super">13</hi> The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy. <hi type="super">14</hi> I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment <hi type="italic">was</hi> as a robe and a diadem. <hi type="super">15</hi> I was eyes to the blind, and feet <hi type="italic">was</hi> I to the lame. <hi type="super">16</hi> I <hi type="italic">was</hi> a father to the poor: and the cause <hi type="italic">which</hi> I knew not I searched out. <hi type="super">17</hi> And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth. <div eID="gen9950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9951" type="x-p"/> We have here Job in a post of honour and power. Though he had comfort enough in his own house, yet he did not confine himself to that. We are not born for ourselves, but for the public. When any business was to be done in the gate, the place of judgment, Job <hi type="italic">went out to</hi> it <hi type="italic">through the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.29.7">v. 7</reference>), not in an affectation of pomp, but in an affection to justice. Observe, Judgment was administered in the gate, in the street, in the places of concourse, to which every man might have a free access, that every one who would might be a witness to all that was said and done, and that when judgment was given against the guilty others might hear and fear. Job being a prince, a judge, a magistrate, a man in authority, among the children of the east, we are here told, <div eID="gen9951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9952" type="x-p"/> I. What a profound respect was paid to him by all sorts of people, not only for the dignity of his place, but for his personal merit, his eminent prudence, integrity, and good management. 1. The people honoured him and stood in awe of him, <reference osisRef="Job.29.8">v. 8</reference>. The gravity and majesty of his looks and mien, and his known strictness in animadverting upon every thing that was evil and indecent, commanded all about him into due decorum. <hi type="italic">The young men,</hi> who could not keep their countenances, or, it may be, were conscious to themselves of something amiss, <hi type="italic">hid themselves,</hi> and got out of his way; <hi type="italic">and the aged,</hi> though they kept their ground, yet would not keep their seats: they <hi type="italic">arose and stood up</hi> to do homage to him; those who expected honour from others gave honour to him. Virtue and piety challenge respect from all, and usually have it; but those that not only <hi type="italic">are</hi> good, but <hi type="italic">do</hi> good, are worthy of double honour. Modesty becomes those that are young and in subjection as much as majesty becomes those that are aged and in power. Honour and fear are due to magistrates, and must be rendered to them, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.7">Rom. xiii. 7</reference>. But, if a great and good man was thus reverenced, how is the great and good God to be feared! 2. The princes and nobles paid great deference to him, <reference osisRef="Job.29.9-Job.29.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Some think that these were inferior magistrates under him, and that the respect they paid him was due to his place, as their sovereign and supreme. It should rather seem that they were his equals in place, and joined in commission with him, and that the peculiar honour they gave him was gained by his extraordinary abilities and services. It was agreed that he excelled them all in quickness of apprehension, soundness of judgment, closeness of application, clearness and copiousness of expression; and therefore he was among his fellows an oracle of law, and counsel, and justice, and what he said all attended to and acquiesced in. When he came into court, especially when he stood up to speak to any business, <hi type="italic">the princes refrained talking, the nobles held their peace,</hi> that they might the more diligently hearken to what he said and might be sure to understand his meaning. Those that had been forward to speak their own thoughts, loved to hear themselves talk, and cared not much what any body else said, yet, when it came to Job's turn to speak, were as desirous to know his thoughts as ever they had been to vent their own. Those that suspected their own judgment were satisfied in his, and admired with what dexterity he split the hair and untied the knots which puzzled them and which they knew not what to make of. When the princes and nobles wrangled among themselves all agreed to refer the matters in dispute to Job and to abide by his judgment. Happy the men that are blessed with such eminent gifts as these; they have great opportunities of honouring God and doing good, but have great need to watch against pride. Happy the people that are blessed with such eminent men; it is a token for good to them. <div eID="gen9952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9953" type="x-p"/> II. What a great deal of good he did in his place. He was very serviceable to his country with the power he had; and here we shall see what it was which Job valued himself by in the day of his prosperity. It is natural to men to have some value for themselves, and we may judge something of our own character by observing what that is upon which we value ourselves. Job valued himself, not by the honour of his family, the great estate he had, his large income, his full table, the many servants he had at his command, the ensigns of his dignity, his equipage and retinue, the splendid entertainments he gave, and the court that was made to him, but by his usefulness. Goodness is God's glory, and it will be ours; if we are merciful as God is, we are perfect as he is. <div eID="gen9953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9954" type="x-p"/> 1. He valued himself by the interest he had in the esteem, affections, and prayers, of sober people; not by the studied panegyrics of the wits and poets, but the unconstrained praises of all about him. All that heard what he said, and saw what he did, how he laid out himself for the public good with all the authority and tender affection of a father to his country, blessed him, and gave witness to him, <reference osisRef="Job.29.11">v. 11</reference>. Many a good word they said of him, and many a good prayer they put up for him. He did not think it an honour to make every body fear him (<hi type="italic">Oderint dum metuant—Let them hate, provided they also fear</hi>) nor to be arbitrary, and to have his own will and way, not caring what people said of him; but, like Mordecai, to be <hi type="italic">accepted of the multitude of his brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.10.3">Esth. x. 3</reference>. He did not so much value the applauses of those at a distance as the attestations of those that were the witnesses of his conduct, that constantly attended him, saw him, and heard him, and could speak of their own knowledge, especially theirs who had themselves been the better for him and could speak by their own experience: such was the blessing of him who was ready to perish (<reference osisRef="Job.29.13">v. 13</reference>) and who by Job's means was rescued from perishing. Let great men, and men of estates, thus do good, and they shall have praise of the same; and let those who have good done to them look upon it as a just debt they owe to their protectors and benefactors to bless them and give witness to them, to use their interest on earth for their honour and in heaven for their comfort, to praise them and pray for them. Those are ungrateful indeed who grudge these small returns. <div eID="gen9954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9955" type="x-p"/> 2. He valued himself by the care he took of those that were least able to help themselves, the poor and the needy, the widows and fatherless, the blind and the lame, who could not be supposed either to merit his favour or ever to be in a capacity to recompense it. (1.) If the poor were injured or oppressed, they might cry to Job, and, if he found the allegations of their petitions true, they had not only his ear and his bowels, but his hand too: He <hi type="italic">delivered the poor that cried</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.29.12">v. 12</reference>) and would not suffer them to be trampled upon and run down. Nay (<reference osisRef="Job.29.16">v. 16</reference>), he was <hi type="italic">a father to the poor,</hi> not only a judge to protect them and to see that they were not wronged, but a father to provide for them and to see that they did not want, to counsel and direct them, and to appear and act for them upon all occasions. It is no disparagement to the son of a prince to be a father to the poor. (2.) The fatherless that had none to help them found Job ready to help them, and, if they were in straits, to deliver them. He helped them to make the best of what little they had, helped them to pay what they owed and to get in what was owing to them, helped them out into the world, helped them into business, helped them to it, and helped them in it; thus should the fatherless be helped. (3.) Those that were ready to perish he saved from perishing, relieving those that were hungry and ready to perish for want, taking care of those that were sick, that were outcasts, that were falsely accused, or in danger of being turned out of their estates unjustly, or, upon any other account, were ready to perish. The extremity of the peril, as it quickened Job to appear the more vigorously for them, so it made his seasonable kindness the more affecting and the more obliging, and brought their blessings the more abundantly upon him. (4.) The widows that were sighing for grief, and trembling for fear, he made to sing for joy, so carefully did he protect them and provide for them, and so heartily did he espouse their interest. It is a pleasure to a good man, and should be so to a great man, to give those occasion to rejoice that are most acquainted with grief. (5.) Those that were upon any account at a loss Job gave suitable and seasonable relief to (<reference osisRef="Job.29.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was eyes to the blind,</hi> counselling and advising those for the best that knew not what to do, and <hi type="italic">feet to the lame,</hi> assisting those with money and friends that knew what they should do, but knew not how to compass it. Those we best help whom we help out in that very thing wherein they are defective and most need help. We may come to be blind or lame ourselves, and therefore should pity and succour those that are so, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.3-Isa.35.4">Isa. xxxv. 3, 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.13">Heb. xii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen9955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9956" type="x-p"/> 3. He valued himself by the conscience he made of justice and equity in all his proceedings. His friends had unjustly censured him as an oppressor. "So far from that," says he, "I always made it my business to maintain and support right." (1.) He devoted himself to the administration of justice (<reference osisRef="Job.29.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I put on righteousness and it clothed me,</hi> that is, he had an habitual disposition to execute justice and put on a fixed resolution to do it. It was <hi type="italic">the girdle of his lions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">Isa. xi. 5</reference>. It kept him tight and steady in all his motions. He always appeared in it, as in his clothing, and never without it. Righteousness will clothe those that put it on; it will keep them warm, and be comfortable to them; it will keep them safe, and fence them against the injuries of the season; it will adorn them, and recommend them to the favour both of God and man. (2.) He took pleasure in it, and, as I may say, a holy delight. He looked upon it as his greatest glory to do justice to all and injury to none: <hi type="italic">My judgment was as a robe and a diadem.</hi> Perhaps he did not himself wear a robe and a diadem; he was very indifferent to those ensigns of honour; those were most fond of them who had least intrinsic worth to recommend them. But the settled principles of justice, by which he was governed and did govern, were to him instead of all those ornaments. If a magistrate do the duty of his place, that is an honour to him far beyond his gold or purple, and should be, accordingly, his delight; and truly if he do not make conscience of his duty, and in some measure answer the end of his elevation, his robe and diadem, his gown and cap, his sword and mace, are but a reproach, like the purple robe and crown of thorns with which the Jews studied to ridicule our Saviour; for, as clothes on a dead man will never make him warm, so robes on a base man will never make him honourable. (3.) He took pains in the business of his place (<reference osisRef="Job.29.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The cause which I knew not I searched out.</hi> He diligently enquired into the matters of fact, patiently and impartially heard both sides, set every thing in its true light, and cleared it from false colours; he laid all circumstances together, that he might find out the truth and the merits of every cause, and then, and not until then, gave judgment upon it. He never answered a matter before he heard it, nor did he judge a man to be righteous, however he seemed, for his being <hi type="italic">first in his own cause,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.17">Prov. xviii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen9956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9957" type="x-p"/> 4. He valued himself by the check he gave to the violence of proud and evil men (<reference osisRef="Job.29.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">I broke the jaws of the wicked.</hi> He does not say that he broke their necks. He did not take away their lives, but he broke their jaws, he took away their power of doing mischief; he humbled them, mortified them, and curbed their insolence, and so plucked the spoil out of their teeth, delivered the persons and estates of honest men from being made a prey of by them. When they had got the spoil between their teeth, and were greedily swallowing it down, he bravely rescued it, as David did the lamb out of the mouth of the lion, not fearing, though they roared and raged like a lion disappointed of his prey. Good magistrates must thus be a terror and restraint to evil-doers and a protection to the innocent, and, in order to this, they have need to arm themselves with zeal, and resolution, and an undaunted courage. A judge upon the bench has as much need to be bold and brave as a commander in the field.
entries.f8a1a9f02c70b5bfcf8c2807724c010556c8cb13: <div eID="gen9957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9958" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then I said, I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply <hi type="italic">my</hi> days as the sand. <hi type="super">19</hi> My root <hi type="italic">was</hi> spread out by the waters, and the dew lay all night upon my branch. <hi type="super">20</hi> My glory <hi type="italic">was</hi> fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand. <hi type="super">21</hi> Unto me <hi type="italic">men</hi> gave ear, and waited, and kept silence at my counsel. <hi type="super">22</hi> After my words they spake not again; and my speech dropped upon them. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they waited for me as for the rain; and they opened their mouth wide <hi type="italic">as</hi> for the latter rain. <hi type="super">24</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> I laughed on them, they believed <hi type="italic">it</hi> not; and the light of my countenance they cast not down. <hi type="super">25</hi> I chose out their way, and sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one <hi type="italic">that</hi> comforteth the mourners. <div eID="gen9958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9959" type="x-p"/> That which crowned Job's prosperity was the pleasing prospect he had of the continuance of it. Though he knew, in general, that he was liable to trouble, and therefore was not secure (<reference osisRef="Job.3.26">ch. iii. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">I was not in safety, neither had I rest</hi>), yet he had no particular occasion for fear, but as much reason as ever any man had to count upon the lengthening out of his tranquility. <div eID="gen9959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9960" type="x-p"/> I. See here what his thoughts were in his prosperity (<reference osisRef="Job.29.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then I said, I shall die in my nest.</hi> Having made himself a warm and easy nest, he hoped nothing would disturb him in it, nor remove him out of it, till death removed him. He knew he had never stolen any coal from the altar which might fire his nest; he saw no storm arising to shake down his nest; and therefore concluded, <hi type="italic">To morrow shall be as this day;</hi> as David (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Ps. xxx. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">My mountain stands strong, and shall not be moved.</hi> Observe, 1. In the midst of his prosperity he thought of dying, and the thought was not uneasy to him. He knew that, though his nest was high, it did not set him out of the reach of the darts of death. 2. Yet he flattered himself with vain hopes, (1.) That he should live long, should <hi type="italic">multiply his days as the sand.</hi> He means as the sand on the sea-shore; whereas we should rather reckon our days by the sand in the hourglass, which will have run out in a little time. See how apt even good people are to think of death as a thing at a distance, and to put far from them that evil day, which will really be to them a good day. (2.) That he should die in the same prosperous state in which he had lived. If such an expectation as this arise from a lively faith in the providence and promise of God, it is well, but if from a conceit of our own wisdom, and the stability of these earthly things, it is ill-grounded and turns into sin. We hope Job's confidence was like David's (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Ps. xxvii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whom shall I fear?),</hi> not like the rich fool's (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">Luke xii. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease.</hi> <div eID="gen9960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9961" type="x-p"/> II. See what was the ground of these thoughts. <div eID="gen9961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9962" type="x-p"/> 1. If he looked at home, he found he had a good foundation. His stock was all his own, and none of all his neighbours had any demand upon him. He found no bodily distemper growing upon him; his estate did not lie under any incumbrance; nor was he sensible of any worm at the root of it. He was getting forward in his affairs, and not going behind-hand; he lost no reputation, but gained rather; he knew no rival that threatened either to eclipse his honour or abridge his power. See how he describes this, <reference osisRef="Job.29.19-Job.29.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. He was like a tree whose root is not only spread out, which fixes it and keeps it firm, so that it is in no danger of being overturned, but <hi type="italic">spread out by the waters,</hi> which feed it, and make it fruitful and flourishing, so that it is in no danger of withering. And, as he thought himself blessed with the fatness of the earth, so also with the kind influences of heaven too; for the <hi type="italic">dew lay all night upon his branch.</hi> Providence favoured him, and made all his enjoyments comfortable and all his enterprises successful. Let none think to support their prosperity with what they draw from this earth without that blessing which is derived from above. God's favour being continued to Job, in the virtue of that his glory was still fresh in him. Those about him had still something new to say in his praise, and needed not to repeat the old stories: and it is only by constant goodness that men's glory is thus preserved fresh and kept from withering and growing stale. His <hi type="italic">bow</hi> also <hi type="italic">was renewed in his hand,</hi> that is, his power to protect himself and annoy those that assailed him still increased, so that he thought he had as little reason as any man to fear the insults of the Sabeans and Chaldeans. <div eID="gen9962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9963" type="x-p"/> 2. If he looked abroad, he found he had a good interest and well confirmed. As he had no reason to dread the power of his enemies, so neither had he any reason to distrust the fidelity of his friends. To the last moment of his prosperity they continued their respect to him and their dependence on him. What had he to fear who so gave counsel as in effect to give law to all his neighbours? Nothing surely could be done against him when really nothing was done without him. <div eID="gen9963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9964" type="x-p"/> (1.) He was the oracle of his country. He was consulted as an oracle, and his dictates were acquiesced in as oracles, <reference osisRef="Job.29.21">v. 21</reference>. When others could not be heard all men <hi type="italic">gave ear</hi> to him, <hi type="italic">and kept silence at his counsel,</hi> knowing that, as nothing could be said against it, so nothing needed to be added to it. And therefore, <hi type="italic">after his words, they spoke not again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.29.22">v. 22</reference>. Why should men meddle with a subject that has already been exhausted? <div eID="gen9964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9965" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was the darling of his country. All about him were well pleased with every thing he said and did, as David's people were with him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.36">2 Sam. iii. 36</reference>. He had the hearts and affections of all his neighbours, all his servants, tenants, subjects; never was man so much admired nor so well beloved. [1.] Those were thought happy to whom he spoke, and they thought themselves so. Never were the dews of heaven so acceptable to the parched ground as his wise discourses were to those that attended on them, especially to those to whom they were particularly accommodated and directed. His speech dropped upon them, and they waited for its as for the rain (<reference osisRef="Job.29.22-Job.29.23">v. 22, 23</reference>), wondering at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth, catching at them, laying hold on them, and treasuring them up as apophthegms. His servants that stood continually before him to hear his wisdom would not have envied Solomon's. Those are wise, or are likely to be so, that know how to value wise discourse, that wish for it, and wait for it, and drink it in as the earth does <hi type="italic">the rain that comes often upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.7">Heb. vi. 7</reference>. And those who have such an interest as Job had in the esteem of others whose <hi type="italic">ipse dixit—bare assertion</hi> goes so far, as they have a great opportunity of doing good, so they must take great care lest they do hurt, for a bad word out of their mouths is very infectious. [2.] Much more happy were those thought on whom he smiled, and they thought themselves so, <reference osisRef="Job.29.24">v. 24</reference>. "<hi type="italic">If I laughed on them,</hi> designing thereby to show myself pleased in them, or pleasant with them, it was such a favour that <hi type="italic">they believed it not</hi> for joy," or because it was so rare a thing to see this grave man smile. <hi type="italic">Many seek the ruler's favour.</hi> Job was a ruler whose favour was courted and valued at a high rate. He to whom a great prince gave a kiss was envied by another to whom he only gave a golden cup. Familiarity often breeds contempt; but if Job at any time saw fit, for his own diversion, to make himself free with those about him, yet it did not in the least diminish the veneration they had for him: <hi type="italic">The light of his countenance they cast not down.</hi> So wisely did he dispense his favours as not to make them cheap, and so wisely did they receive them as not to make themselves unworthy of them another time. <div eID="gen9965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9966" type="x-p"/> (3.) He was the sovereign of his country, <reference osisRef="Job.29.25">v. 25</reference>. He <hi type="italic">chose out their way,</hi> sat at the helm, and steered for them, all referring themselves to his conduct and submitting themselves to his command. To this perhaps, in many countries, monarchy owed its rise: such a man as Job, that so far excelled all his neighbours in wisdom and integrity, could not but sit chief, and the fool will, of course, be servant to the wise in heart: and, if the wisdom did but for a while run in the blood, the honour and power would certainly attend it and so by degrees become hereditary. Two things recommended Job to the sovereignty:—[1.] That he had the authority of a commander or general. He <hi type="italic">dwelt as a king in the army,</hi> giving orders which were not to be disputed. Every one that has the spirit of wisdom has not the spirit of government, but Job had both, and, when there was occasion, could assume state, as the king in the army does, and say, "Go," "Come," and "Do this," <reference osisRef="Matt.8.9">Matt. viii. 9</reference>. [2.] That yet he had the tenderness of a comforter. He was as ready to succour those in distress as if it had been his office to comfort the mourners. Eliphaz himself owned he had been very good in that respect (<reference osisRef="Job.4.3">ch. iv. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast strengthened the weak hands.</hi> And this he now reflected upon with pleasure, when he was himself a mourner. But we find it easier to comfort others with the comforts wherewith we ourselves have been formerly comforted than to comfort ourselves with those comforts wherewith we have formerly comforted others. <div eID="gen9966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9967" type="x-p"/> I know not but we may look upon Job as a type and figure of Christ in his power and prosperity. Our Lord Jesus is such a King as Job was, the poor man's King, who loves righteousness and hates iniquity, and upon whom the blessing of a world ready to perish comes; see <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2-Ps.72.17">Ps. lxxii. 2</reference>, &c. To him therefore let us give ear, and let him sit chief in our hearts.  <chapter eID="Job.29"/> <div eID="gen9967" type="x-p"/>

entries.aa45f837fc48f0b972eaff26ad23c3ef61569803: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5068"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <div sID="gen7509" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.29.1-Job.29.25">Job 29:1-25</reference>.<div eID="gen7509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5068"/>1. Job pauses for a reply. None being made, he proceeds to illustrate the mysteriousness of God's dealings, as set forth (<reference osisRef="Job.28.1-Job.28.28">Job 28:1-28</reference>) by his own case. <div eID="gen7510" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae90742bfb119a7bc909cb1d1b9d71ec408c006f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5069"/><div sID="gen7511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5069"/><hi type="bold">2. preserved me--</hi>from calamity. <div eID="gen7511" type="x-p"/>
entries.7da4b957531b6192adda8b3d3a1c6c207dbfd5db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5070"/><div sID="gen7512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5070"/><hi type="bold">3. candle--</hi>when His favor shone on me (see on <reference osisRef="Job.18.6">Job 18:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference>).<div eID="gen7512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>By His safeguard I passed secure through dangers. Perhaps alluding to the lights carried before caravans in nightly travels through deserts [Noyes]. <div eID="gen7513" type="x-p"/>
entries.892ba3fbc3b298712fe18aae4edaf71db6f60853: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5071"/><div sID="gen7514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5071"/><hi type="bold">4. youth--</hi>literally, "autumn"; the time of the ripe fruits of my prosperity. Applied to youth, as the Orientalists began their year with autumn, the most temperate season in the East.<div eID="gen7514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">secret--</hi>when the intimate friendship of God rested on my tent (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pr 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Ge 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">Joh 15:15</reference>). The Hebrew often means a divan for deliberation. <div eID="gen7515" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ad5cb17e6cbbad7c650bed37dc0313fcbc12c72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5072"/><div sID="gen7516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5072"/><hi type="bold">6. butter--</hi>rather, "cream," literally, "thick milk." Wherever I turned my steps, the richest milk and oil flowed in to me abundantly. Image from pastoral life.<div eID="gen7516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">When I washed my steps--</hi>Literal washing of the feet in milk is not meant, as the second clause shows; Margin, "with me," that is, "near" my path, wherever I walked (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>). Olives amidst rocks yield the best oil. Oil in the East is used for food, light, anointing, and medicine. <div eID="gen7517" type="x-p"/>
entries.2247f81d326fa20c54b84d24b9ec1b33c79e761a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5073"/><div sID="gen7518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5073"/>7-10. The great influence Job had over young and old, and noblemen.<div eID="gen7518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through ... street!--</hi>rather, When I went out of my house, in the country (see <reference osisRef="Job.1.1">Job 1:1</reference>, prologue) to the gate (ascending), up to the city (which was on elevated ground), and when I prepared my (judicial) seat in the market place. The market place was the place of judgment, at the gate or propylæa of the city, such as is found in the remains of Nineveh and Persepolis (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.14">Is 59:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.11">Psa 55:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">127:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7519" type="x-p"/>
entries.689ebb3a5e9bac6bd14b24a278e763614f7b7eb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5077"/><div sID="gen7525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5077"/><hi type="bold">11. blessed--</hi>extolled my virtues (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.28">Pr 31:28</reference>). Omit "me" after "heard"; whoever heard of me (in general, not in the market place, <reference osisRef="Job.29.7-Job.29.10">Job 29:7-10</reference>) praised me.<div eID="gen7525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gave witness--</hi>to my honorable character. Image from a court of justice (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Lu 4:22</reference>).<div eID="gen7526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the eye--</hi>that is, "face to face"; antithesis to<div eID="gen7527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ear--</hi>that is, report of me. <div eID="gen7528" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef331e1ab979d7b27ade11eb8a39f4ed9c994811: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5078"/><div sID="gen7529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5078"/>12-17. The grounds on which Job was praised (<reference osisRef="Job.29.11">Job 29:11</reference>), his helping the afflicted (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.12">Psa 72:12</reference>) who cried to him for help, as a judge, or as one possessed of means of charity. Translate: "The fatherless who had none to help him." <div eID="gen7529" type="x-p"/>
entries.02d1adf3635c2c3e645512ffdc551e899f761422: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5084"/><div sID="gen7540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5084"/><hi type="bold">18. I said--</hi>in my heart (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Psa 30:6</reference>).<div eID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>rather, "with my nest"; as the second clause refers to long life. Instead of my family dying before me, as now, I shall live so long as to die with them: proverbial for long life. Job did realize his hope (<reference osisRef="Job.42.16">Job 42:16</reference>). However, in the bosom of my family, gives a good sense (<reference osisRef="Num.24.21">Nu 24:21</reference>; Ob 4). Use "nest" for a secure dwelling.<div eID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Ge 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.9">Ha 1:9</reference>). But the Septuagint and Vulgate, and Jewish interpreters, favor the translation, "the phoenix bird." "Nest" in the parallel clause supports the reference to a bird. "Sand" for multitude, applies to men, rather than to years. The myth was, that the phoenix sprang from a nest of myrrh, made by his father before death, and that he then came from Arabia (Job's country) to Heliopolis (the city of the Sun) in Egypt, once in every five hundred years, and there burnt his father [Herodotus, 2:73]. Modern research has shown that this was the Egyptian mode of representing hieroglyphically a particular chronological era or cycle. The death and revival every five hundred years, and the reference to the sun, implies such a grand cycle commencing afresh from the same point in relation to the sun from which the previous one started. Job probably refers to this. <div eID="gen7542" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9ec5c311babc98a5a85668f50004570f45dfbc6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5085"/><div sID="gen7543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5085"/>19. Literally, "opened to the waters." Opposed to <reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job 18:16</reference>. Vigorous health. <div eID="gen7543" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2696804e3cd1285bc4e4106d1e4b8953331a973: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5086"/><div sID="gen7544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5086"/>20. My renown, like my bodily health, was continually fresh.<div eID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow--</hi>Metaphor from war, for, my strength, which gains me "renown," was ever renewed (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">Jr 49:35</reference>). <div eID="gen7545" type="x-p"/>
entries.51902251ea2010de700bd9ae37f4b6508c447ff3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5087"/><div sID="gen7546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5087"/>21. Job reverts with peculiar pleasure to his former dignity in assemblies (<reference osisRef="Job.29.7-Job.29.10">Job 29:7-10</reference>). <div eID="gen7546" type="x-p"/>
entries.cecdef60ad8d38aebcdf196d04afbc629f3cb585: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5088"/><div sID="gen7547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5088"/><hi type="bold">22. not again--</hi>did not contradict me.<div eID="gen7547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dropped--</hi>affected their minds, as the genial rain does the soil on which it gently drops (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.16">Am 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">So 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7548" type="x-p"/>
entries.07f7c7f0e16890a51e8df5a43b73547e76001de7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5089"/><div sID="gen7549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5089"/>23. Image of <reference osisRef="Job.29.22">Job 29:22</reference> continued. They waited for my salutary counsel, as the dry soil does for the refreshing rain.<div eID="gen7549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opened ... mouth--</hi>panted for; Oriental image (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.131">Psa 119:131</reference>). The "early rain" is in autumn and onwards, while the seed is being sown. The "latter rain" is in March, and brings forward the harvest, which ripens in May or June. Between the early and latter rains, some rain falls, but not in such quantities as those rains. Between March and October no rain falls (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">De 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.7">Jas 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7550" type="x-p"/>
entries.4026574acb315d2117fab7c6ce1fad1384cb0953: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5090"/><div sID="gen7551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5090"/>24. When I relaxed from my wonted gravity (a virtue much esteemed in the East) and smiled, they could hardly credit it; and yet, notwithstanding my condescension, they did not cast aside reverence for my gravity. But the parallelism is better in Umbreit's translation, "I smiled kindly on those who trusted not," that is, in times of danger I cheered those in despondency. And they could not cast down (by their despondency) my serenity of countenance (flowing from trust in God) (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Pr 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>). The opposite phrase (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.5">Ge 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.6">6</reference>). "Gravity" cannot well be meant by "light of countenance." <div eID="gen7551" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddaad15edd022159cb928f2a66eda9abb6e2ba0d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5091"/><div sID="gen7552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5091"/><hi type="bold">25. I chose out their way--</hi>that is, I willingly went up to their assembly (from my country residence, <reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job 29:7</reference>).<div eID="gen7552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the army--</hi>as a king supreme in the midst of his army.<div eID="gen7553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comforteth the mourners--</hi>Here again Job unconsciously foreshadows Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Is 61:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">3</reference>). Job's afflictions, as those of Jesus Christ, were fitting him for the office hereafter (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Is 50:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.18">He 2:18</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.29"/>

entries.a82eb88ff54a9a68f706866fa7f2659a76ecbfc1: <div eID="gen17309" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> Job laments his present condition, and gives an affecting account of his former prosperity, having property in abundance, being surrounded by a numerous family, and enjoying every mark of the approbation of God, <reference osisRef="Job.29.1-Job.29.6">Job 29:1-6</reference>. Speaks of the respect he had from the young, <reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>; and from the nobles, <reference osisRef="Job.29.9">Job 29:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.10">Job 29:10</reference>. Details his conduct as a magistrate and judge in supporting the poor, and repressing the wicked, <reference osisRef="Job.29.11-Job.29.17">Job 29:11-17</reference>; his confidence, general prosperity, and respect, <reference osisRef="Job.29.18-Job.29.25">Job 29:18-25</reference>.
entries.1feece04afd4a4b73ffc41dcb963f36429747bef: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> O that I were as in months past - Job seems here to make an apology for his complaints, by taking a view of his former prosperity, which was very great, but was now entirely at an end. He shows that it was not removed because of any bad use he had made of it; and describes how he behaved himself before God and man, and how much, for justice, benevolence, and mercy, he was esteemed and honored by the wise and good. <div eID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> Preserved me - Kept, guarded, and watched over me.
entries.3ce9fb18fee14137c0749e4f59950eb66cc896b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17315" type="x-p"/> When his candle shined upon my head - Alluding most probably to the custom of illuminating festival or assembly rooms by lamps pendant from the ceiling. These shone literally on the heads of the guests. <div eID="gen17315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> By his light I walked through darkness - His light - prosperity and peace - continued to illuminate my way. If adversity came, I had always the light of God to direct me. Almost all the nations of the world have represented their great men as having a nimbus or Divine glory about their heads, which not only signified the honor they had, but was also an emblem of the inspiration of the Almighty.
entries.9f9c2ec719cea7daebea2e2df8e53b1b7027d7d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17317" type="x-p"/> The days of my youth - The original word rather means in the days of my winter, חרפי charpi, from חרף charaph, "to strip or make bare." Mr. Harmer supposes the rainy season is intended, when the fields, etc., parched up by long drought, are revived by the plentiful showers. Mr. Good thinks the word as found in the Arabic, which means top or summit, and which he translates perfection, is that which should be preferred. Others think the autumnal state is meant, when he was loaded with prosperity, as the trees are with ripe fruit. <div eID="gen17317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17318" type="x-p"/> The secret of God was upon my tabernacle - בסוד אלוה besod Eloah, "the secret assembly of God," meaning probably the same thing that is spoken of in the beginning of this book, the sons of God, the devout people, presenting themselves before God. It is not unlikely that such a secret assembly of God Job had in his own house; where he tells us, in the next verse, "The Almighty was with him, and his children were about him." Mr. Good translates differently: When God fortified my tent over me; supposing that the Hebrew סוד sod is the Arabic sud, "a barrier or fortification." Either will make a good sense.
entries.3d50e2e05151be60cf62ea07d036e8a23f21151e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17319" type="x-p"/> Washed my steps with butter - See the note on <reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference>.
entries.fe87a2803f57b17f2f50806c2f00c44459efaf14: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17320" type="x-p"/> When I went out to the gate - Courts of justice were held at the gates or entrances of the cities of the East; and Job, being an emir, was supreme magistrate: and here he speaks of his going to the gate to administer justice. <div eID="gen17320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17321" type="x-p"/> I prepared my seat in the street - I administered judgment openly, in the most public manner, and none could say that I, in any case, perverted justice. Mr. Good translates: - "As I went forth the city rejoiced at me, as I took my seat abroad."
entries.871a139f1ce20e0320c8487f5018ccb77ea05ae3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17322" type="x-p"/> The young men saw me, and hid themselves - From all classes of persons I had the most marked respect. The Young, through modesty and bashfulness, shrunk back, and were afraid to meet the eye of their prince; and the Aged rose from their seats when I entered the place of judgment. These were the elders of the people, who also sat with the judge, and assisted in all legal cases.
entries.136d551db376b05c8b7096f73b8ad2ad3af2a015: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17323" type="x-p"/> The princes refrained talking - They never ventured an opinion in opposition to mine; so fully were they persuaded of the justice and integrity of my decision.
entries.5fda1076276bcbe3cd414a3dd1de7cd02c20323e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17324" type="x-p"/> The nobles held their peace - Princes שרים sarim, and Nobles, נגידים negidim, must have been two different classes of the great men of Idumea. שר sar, Prince, director, or ruler, was probably the head of a township, or what we would call a magistrate of a particular district. נגיד nagid, a Noble, or one of those who had the privilege of standing before, or in the presence of, the chief ruler. The participle נגד neged is frequently used to signify before, in the presence of, publicly, openly. And on this account, it is most likely that the noun means one of those nobles or counsellors who were always admitted to the royal presence. Mr. Good thinks that renowned speakers or eminent orators are meant: and others have embraced the same opinion. Job here intimates that his judgment was so sound, his decisions so accredited, and his reasoning power so great, that every person paid him the utmost deference.
entries.4770beb5e11b35692333faa266d9f3f61c895381: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17325" type="x-p"/> When the ear heard me - This and the six following verses present us with a fine exhibition of a man full of benevolence and charity, acting up to the highest dictates of those principles, and rendering the miserable of all descriptions happy, by the constant exercise of his unconfined philanthropy.
entries.c86a2a1a1725e1a03f2f22b483c4668c587aeb17: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17326" type="x-p"/> Because I delivered the poor that cried - This appears to be intended as a refutation of the charges produced by Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.22.5-Job.22.10">Job 22:5-10</reference>, to confute which Job appeals to facts, and to public testimony.
entries.486c683f6896bc48d666174657c752f178b41650: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17327" type="x-p"/> I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame - Alluding probably to the difficulty of travelling in the Arabian deserts. I was eyes to the blind - those who did not know the way, I furnished with guides. I was feet to the lame - those who were worn out, and incapable of walking, I set forward on my camels, etc.
entries.33e87772dafd995c6b466d6c06139ebf48d6984c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17328" type="x-p"/> The cause which I knew not I searched out - When any thing difficult occurred, I did not give it a slight consideration; I examined it to the bottom, whatever pain, time, and trouble it cost me, that I might not pronounce a hasty judgment.
entries.126838c4fd5275a05c3e88c9225919247cdee2c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17329" type="x-p"/> I brake the jaws of the wicked - A metaphor taken from hunting. A beast of prey had entered into the fold, and carried off a sheep. "The huntsman comes, assails the wicked beast, breaks his jaws, and delivers the spoil out of his teeth. See the case <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.37">1Sam 17:34-37</reference> (note).
entries.d65938c7e6b9d3ec9a4972c1e8e049b63389ef18: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17330" type="x-p"/> I shall die in my nest - As I endeavored to live soberly and temperately, fearing God, and departing from evil, endeavoring to promote the welfare of all around me, it was natural for me to conclude that I should live long, be very prosperous, and see my posterity multiply as the sands on the seashore.
entries.8db53a2a37c56ee3712cfb4f8311022c5185441b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen17330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17331" type="x-p"/> My root was spread out by the waters - A metaphor taken from a healthy tree growing beside a rivulet where there is plenty of water; which in consequence flourishes in all seasons; its leaf does not wither, nor its fruit fall off. See <reference osisRef="Psa.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jer 17:8</reference>.
entries.52b2b41a1a7fb605023a4ed521076a8da186f671: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17332" type="x-p"/> My glory was fresh in me - My vegetative power was great; my glory - my splendid blossom, large and mellow fruit, was always in season, and in every season. <div eID="gen17332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17333" type="x-p"/> My bow was renewed - I was never without means to accomplish all my wishes. I had prosperity everywhere.
entries.2494b48bd21f7e88506bb66d0a88713a6b8082c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17334" type="x-p"/> Unto me men gave ear - The same idea as in <reference osisRef="Job.29.9-Job.29.11">Job 29:9-11</reference>.
entries.c1d689afcd6c59b41ecffd46586d193898c1a191: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17335" type="x-p"/> My speech dropped upon them - It descended as refreshing dew; they were encouraged, comforted, and strengthened by it.
entries.981ebfd451ec5e73dee5ddccbc5af61b5932094d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17336" type="x-p"/> They waited for me as for the rain - The idea continued. They longed as much to hear me speak, to receive my counsel and my decisions, as the thirsty land does for refreshing waters. <div eID="gen17336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17337" type="x-p"/> They opened their mouth wide - A metaphor taken from ground chapped with long drought. <div eID="gen17337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17338" type="x-p"/> The latter rain - The rain that falls a little before harvest, in order to fill and perfect the grain. The former rain is that which falls about seed-time, or in spring, in order to impregnate and swell the seed, and moisten the earth to produce its nourishment.
entries.d486d0b4ce442645371cf78a1e96b58deb3de5d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17339" type="x-p"/> I laughed on them, they believed it not - Similar to that expression in the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.41">Luk 24:41</reference> : And while they believed not for joy, and wondered, he said - . Our version is sufficiently perspicuous, and gives the true sense of the original, only it should be read in the indicative and not in the subjunctive mood: I laughed on them - they believed it not. We have a similar phrase: The news was too good to be true. <div eID="gen17339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17340" type="x-p"/> The light of my countenance - This evidence of my benevolence and regard. A smile is, metaphorically, the light of the countenance. <div eID="gen17340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17341" type="x-p"/> They cast not down - They gave me no occasion to change my sentiments or feelings towards them. I could still smile upon them, and they were then worthy of my approbation. Their change he refers to in the beginning of the next chapter.
entries.07c87e9b3fbc66a724650f4435cfe480abf3b57d: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen17341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17342" type="x-p"/> I chose out their way, and sat chief - as a king in the army - I cannot see, with some learned men, that our version of the original is wrong. I have not seen it mended, and I am sure I cannot improve it. The whole verse seems to me to point out Job in his civil, military, and domestic life. As supreme magistrate he chose out their way, adjusted their differences, and sat chief, presiding in all their civil assemblies. As captain general he dwelt as a king in the midst of his troops, preserving order and discipline, and seeing that his fellow soldiers were provided with requisites for their warfare, and the necessaries of life. As a man he did not think himself superior to the meanest offices in domestic life, to relieve or support his fellow creatures; he went about comforting the mourners - visiting the sick and afflicted, and ministering to their wants, and seeing that the wounded were properly attended. Noble Job! Look at him, ye nobles of the earth, ye lieutenants of counties, ye generals of armies, and ye lords of provinces. Look at Job! Imitate his active benevolence, and be healthy and happy. Be as guardian angels in your particular districts, blessing all by your example and your bounty. Send your hunting horses to the plough, your game cocks to the dunghill; and at last live like men and Christians.  <chapter eID="Job.29"/> <div eID="gen17342" type="x-p"/>

entries.3c53096dbe6fa2e7d226805a0c2ded6dfd24aff7: <reference osisRef="Job.29.1-Job.6.1">Job 29:1-6   1</reference>  Then Job continued to take up his proverb, and said:   2  O that I had months like the times of yore, <div eID="gen8112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8113" type="x-p"/> Like the days when Eloah protected me,   3  When He, when His lamp, shone above my head, <div eID="gen8113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8114" type="x-p"/> By His light I went about in the darkness;   4  As I was in the days of my vintage, <div eID="gen8114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8115" type="x-p"/> When the secret of Eloah was over my tent,   5  When the Almighty was still with me, <div eID="gen8115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8116" type="x-p"/> My children round about me;   6  When my steps were bathed in cream, <div eID="gen8116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8117" type="x-p"/> And the rock beside me poured forth streams of oil. <div eID="gen8117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8118" type="x-p"/> Since the optative מי־יתּן (comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.23.3">Job 23:3</reference>) is connected with the acc. of the object desired, <reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job 31:31</reference>, or of that respecting which anything is desired, <reference osisRef="Job.11.5">Job 11:5</reference>, it is in itself possible to explain: who gives (makes) me like the months of yore; but since, when מי־יתּנני occurs elsewhere, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa 27:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer 9:1</reference>, the <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. is meant as the dative (= מי־יתן לי, <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>), it is also here to be explained: who gives me (= O that one would give me, O that I had) like (<hi type="italic">instar</hi>) the months of yore, i.e., months like those of the past, and indeed those that lie far back in the past; for ירחי־קדם means more than עברוּ (אשׁר) ירחים. Job begins to describe the olden times, that he wishes back, with the virtually genitive relative clause: “when Eloah protected me” (Ges. §116, 3). It is impossible to take בּהלּו as <hi type="italic">Hiph.:</hi> when He caused to shine (Targ. בּאנהרוּתיהּ); either בּההלּו (Olsh.) or even בּהלּו (Ew. in his <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>.) ought to be read then. On the other hand, הלּו can be justified as the form for <hi type="italic">inf. Kal</hi> of הלל (to shine, vid., <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">Job 25:5</reference>) with a weakening of the <hi type="italic">a</hi> to <hi type="italic">i</hi> (Ew. §255, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), and the <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. may, according to the syntax, be taken as an anticipatory statement of the object: when it, viz., His light, shone above my head; comp. <reference osisRef="Exod.2.6">Exo 2:6</reference> (him, the boy), <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Isa 17:6</reference> (its, the fruit-tree’s, branches), also <reference osisRef="Isa.29.23">Isa 29:23</reference> (he, his children); and Ew. §309, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, also decides in its favour. Nevertheless it commends itself still more to refer the <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. of בהלו to אלוהּ (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">Isa 60:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>), and to take נרו as a corrective, explanatory permutative: when He, His lamp, shone above my head, as we have translated. One is at any rate reminded of Isa 60 in connection with <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">Job 29:3</reference>; for as בהלו corresponds to יזרח there, so לאורו corresponds to לאורך in the <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">Job 29:3</reference> of the same: by His light I walked in darkness (חשׁך locative = בּחשׁך), i.e., rejoicing in His light, which preserved me from its dangers (straying and falling). <div eID="gen8118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8119" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.29.4">Job 29:4</reference> כּאשׁר is not a particle of time, but of comparison, which was obliged here to stand in the place of the כּ, which is used only as a preposition. And חרפּי (to be written thus, not חרפי with an aspirated )פ may not be translated “(in the days) of my spring,” as Symm. ἐν ἡμέραις νεότητός μου, Jer. <hi type="italic">diebus adolescentiae meae,</hi> and Targ. בּיומי חריפוּתי, whether it be that חריפות here signifies the point, ἀκμή (from חרף, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥrf , acuere</hi>), or the early time (spring time, from חרף, Arab. <hi type="italic">chrf , carpere</hi>). For in reference to agriculture חרף can certainly signify the early half of the year (on this, vid., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, S. 270), inasmuch as sowing and ploughing time in Palestine and Syria is in November and December; wherefore Arab. <hi type="italic">chrı̂f</hi> signifies the early rain or autumn rain; and in Talmudic, חרף, premature (ripe too early), is the opposite of אפל, late, but the derivatives of חרף only obtain this signification <hi type="italic">connotative,</hi> for, according to its proper signification, חרף (Arab. <hi type="italic">chrı̂f</hi> with other forms) is the gathering time, i.e., the time of the fruit harvest (syn. אסיף), while the Hebr. אביב (אב) corresponds to the spring in our sense. If Job meant his youth, he would have said בּימי אבּי, or something similar; but as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.5">Job 29:5</reference></hi> shows, he meant his manhood, and this he calls his autumn as the season of maturity, or rather of the abundance of fruits (Schult.: <hi type="italic">aetatem virilem suis fructibus faetum et exuberantum</hi>),<note placement="foot">The fresh vegetation, indeed, in hotter districts (e.g., in the valley of the Jordan and Euphrates) begins with the arrival of the autumnal rains, but the real spring (comp. Sol 2:11-13) only begins about the vernal equinox, and still later on the mountains. On the contrary, the late summer, קיץ, which passes over into the autumn, חרף, is the season for gathering the fruit. The produce of the fields, garden fruit, and grapes ripen before the commencement of the proper autumn; some (when the land can be irrigated) summer fruits, e.g., <hi type="italic">Dhura</hi> (maize) and melons, in like manner olives and dates, ripen in autumn. Therefore the translation, in the days of my autumn (“of my harvest”), is the only correct one. If חרפּי were intended here in a sense not used elsewhere, it might signify, according to the Arabic with <hi type="italic">h</hi>, “(in the days) of my prosperity,” or ”my power,” or even with Arab. <hi type="italic">ch</hi>, “(in the days) of my youthful vigour;” for <hi type="italic">charâfât</hi> are rash words and deeds, <hi type="italic">charfân</hi> one who says or does anything rash from lightness, the feebleness of old age, etc. (according to Wetzst., very common words in Syria): חרף or חרף, therefore the thoughtlessness of youth, Arab. <hi type="italic">jahl</hi>, i.e., the rash desire of doing something great, which חרף הנפש למות (Jdg 5:18). But it is most secure to go back to חרף, Arab. <hi type="italic">chrf , carpere,</hi> viz., <hi type="italic">fructus</hi>.</note> which, according to Olympiodorus, also with ὅτε ἤμην ἐπιβρίθων ὁδούς (perhaps καρπούς) of the lxx, is what is intended. Then the blessed fellowship of Eloah (סוד, familiarity, confiding, unreserved intercourse, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">Psa 55:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pro 3:32</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>) ruled over his tent; the Almighty was still with him (protecting and blessing him), His נערים were round about him. It certainly does not mean servants (Raschi: משׁרתי), but children (as <reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.5">Job 24:5</reference>); for one expects the mention of the blessing of children first of all (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.3">Psa 127:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">Psa 128:3</reference>). His steps (הליך, ἅπ. λεγ.) bathed then בּחמה = בּחמאה, <reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference> (as שׁלה = שׁאלה,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.17">1Sa 1:17</reference>, and possibly גּוה = גּאוה), and the rocks poured forth, close by him, streams of oil (a figure which reminds one of <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">Deu 32:13</reference>). A rich blessing surrounded him wherever he tarried or went, and flowed to him wonderfully beyond desire and comprehension.
entries.645e0700304bb5a6a586f60709e6e8b035c73ba9: <reference osisRef="Job.29.7-Job.10.7">Job 29:7-10   7</reference>  When I went forth to the gate of the city, <div eID="gen8119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8120" type="x-p"/> Prepared my seat in the market,   8  Then the young men hid themselves as soon as they saw me, <div eID="gen8120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8121" type="x-p"/> And the aged rose up, remained standing.   9  Princes refrained from speaking, <div eID="gen8121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8122" type="x-p"/> And laid their hand on their mouth. 10  The voice of the nobles was hidden, <div eID="gen8122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8123" type="x-p"/> And their tongue clave to their palate. <div eID="gen8123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8124" type="x-p"/> When he left the bounds of his domain, and came into the city, he was everywhere received with the profoundest respect. From the facts of the case, it is inadmissible to translate <hi type="italic">quum egrederer portam</hi> after <reference osisRef="Gen.34.24">Gen 34:24</reference>, comp. <hi type="italic">infra,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.34">Job 31:34</reference>, for the district where Job dwelt is to be thought of as being without a gate. True, he did not dwell with his family in tents, i.e., pavilions of hair, but in houses; he was not a nomad (a wandering herdsman), or what is the same thing, a Beduin, otherwise his children would not have been slain in a stone house, Job 1:19. “The daughter of the duck,” says an Arabian proverb, “is a swimmer,” and the son of a Beduin never dwells in a stone house. He was, however, also, not a citizen, but a <hi type="italic">hadarı̂</hi> (חצרי), i.e., a permanent resident, a large landowner and husbandman. Thus therefore שׁער (for which Ew. after the lxx reads שׁחר: “when I went up early in the morning to the city”) is locative, for שׁערה (comp. צא השּׂדה, go out into the field, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.3">Gen 27:3</reference>): when he went forth to the gate above the city; or even, since it is natural to imagine the city as situated on an eminence: up to the city (so that צאת includes in itself by implication the notion of עלות); not, however: to the gate near the city (Stick., Hahn), since the gate of a city is not situated near the city, but is part of the city itself. The gates of cities and large houses in Western Asia are vaulted entrances, with large recesses on either side, where people congregate for business and negotiations.<note placement="foot">Vid., Layard, <hi type="italic">New Discoveries,</hi> p. 57.</note> <div eID="gen8124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8125" type="x-p"/> The open space at the gate, which here, as in <reference osisRef="Neh.8.1">Neh 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.3">Neh 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.16">Neh 8:16</reference>, is called רחוב, i.e., the open space within the gate and by the gate, was the forum (<reference osisRef="Job.5.4">Job 5:4</reference>).
entries.e4660642001124d60121077cf1748a1b5ff32b2a: <reference osisRef="Job.29.11-Job.14.11">Job 29:11-14 11</reference>  For an ear heard, and called me happy; <div eID="gen8127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8128" type="x-p"/> And an eye saw, and bear witness to me: 12  For I rescued the sufferer who cried for help, <div eID="gen8128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8129" type="x-p"/> And the orphan, and him that had no helper. 13  The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me, <div eID="gen8129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8130" type="x-p"/> And I made the widow’s heart rejoice. 14  I put on justice, and it put me on; <div eID="gen8130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8131" type="x-p"/> As a robe and turban was my integrity. <div eID="gen8131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8132" type="x-p"/> Thus imposing was the impression of his personal appearance wherever he appeared; for (כּי <hi type="italic">explic</hi>.) the fulness of the blessing of the possession of power and of prosperity which he enjoyed was so extraordinary, that one had only to hear of it to call him happy, and that, especially if any one saw it with his own eyes, he was obliged to bear laudatory testimony to him. The <hi type="italic">futt. consec.</hi> affirm what was the inevitable consequence of hearing and seeing; העיד, <hi type="italic">seq. acc.,</hi> is used like הזכּיר in the signification of laudatory recognition. The expression is not brachylogical for ותּעד לּי (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference>); for from 1Ki 21:10, 1Ki 21:13, we perceive that העיד with the <hi type="italic">acc. </hi>of the person signifies to make any one the subject of assertion, whether he be lower or higher in rank (comp. the New Testament word, especially in Luke, μαρτυρεῖσθαι). It was, however, not merely the outward manifestation of his unusual prosperity which called forth such admiration, but his active benevolence united with the abundant resources at his command. For where there was a sufferer who cried for help he, relieved him, especially orphans and those who had no helper. ולא־עזר לו is either a new third object, or a closer definition of what precedes: the orphan and (in this state of orphanhood) helpless one. The latter is more probable both here and in the Salomonic primary passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.12">Psa 72:12</reference>; in the other case ואשׁר אין־עזר לח might be expected.
entries.9bb4114770182be199c65a5649a21a689694180d: <reference osisRef="Job.29.15-Job.17.15">Job 29:15-17 15</reference>  I was eyes to the blind, <div eID="gen8134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> And feet was I to the lame. 16  I was a father to the needy, <div eID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8136" type="x-p"/> And the cause of the unknown I found out, 17  And broke the teeth of the wicked, <div eID="gen8136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8137" type="x-p"/> And I cast the spoil forth out of his teeth. <div eID="gen8137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8138" type="x-p"/> The less it is Job’s purpose here to vindicate himself before the friends, the more forcible is the refutation which the accusations of the most hard-hearted uncharitableness raised against him by them, especially by Eliphaz, Job 22, find everywhere here. His charity relieved the bodily and spiritual wants of others - eyes to the blind (לעוּר with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>), feet to the lame.
