A father was he to the needy, which is expressed by a beautiful play of words, as if it were: the carer for the care-full ones; or what perhaps corresponds to the primary significations of אב and אביון:<note placement="foot">There is an old Arabic defective verb, <hi type="italic">bayya ,</hi> which signifies ”to seek an asylum for one’s self,” e.g., <hi type="italic">anâ baj ,</hi> I come as one seeking protection, a suppliant, in the usual language synon. of Arab. <hi type="italic">dachala ,</hi> and thereby indicating its relationship to the Hebr. בּוא, perhaps the root of בּית (בּתּים), the ת of which would then not be a radical letter, but, as according to Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. in זית, used only in the forming of the word, and the original meaning would be “a refuge.” Traced to a secondary verb, אבה (properly to take up the fugitive, <hi type="italic">qabila - l - bı̂ja</hi>) springing from this primitive verb, אב would originally signify a guardian, protector; and from the fact of this name denoting, according to the form פּעל, properly in general the protecting power, the ideal <hi type="italic">femin</hi>. in אבות (Arab. <hi type="italic">abawât'</hi> and the Arabic dual <hi type="italic">abawain</hi> (properly both guardians), which embraces father and mother, would be explained and justified. Thus the rare phenomenon that the same אבה signifies in Hebr. “to be willing,” and in Arab. “to refuse,” would be solved. The notion of taking up the fugitive would have passed over in the Hebrew, taken according to its positive side, into the notion of being willing, i.e., of receiving and accepting (אבּל, <hi type="italic">qabila ,</hi> e.g., 1Ki 20:8, לא תעבה = <hi type="italic">la taqbal</hi>); in the Arabic, however, taken according to its negative side, as refusing the fugitive to his pursuer, into that of not being willing; and the usage of the language favours this: <hi type="italic">abâhu ‛aleihi ,</hi> he protected him against (Arab. <hi type="italic">'lâ</hi>) the other (refused him to the other); Arab. <hi type="italic">abı̂yun</hi> = <hi type="italic">ma'bin ,</hi> protected, inaccessible to him who longs for it; Arab. <hi type="italic">ibyat ,</hi> the protection, i.e., the retention of the milk in the udder. Hence אביון, from the Hebrew signif. of the verb, signifies one who desires anything, or a needy person, but originally (inasmuch as אבה is connected with Arab. <hi type="italic">byy</hi>) one who needs protection; from the Arabic signif. of Arab. <hi type="italic">'abâ ,</hi> one who restrains himself because he is obliged, one to whom what he wants is denied. To the Arab. <hi type="italic">ibja</hi> (defence, being hindered) corresponds in form the Hebr. אבה, according to which אניות אבה, <reference osisRef="Job.9.26">Job 9:26</reference>, may be understood of ships, which, with all sails set and in all haste, seek the sheltering harbour before the approaching storm. We leave this suggestion for further research to sift and prove. More on Job 34:36. - Wetzst.</note> the protector of those needing (seeking) protection. The unknown he did not regard as those who were nothing to him, but went unselfishly and impartially into the ground of their cause. לא־ידעתּי is an attributive clause, as <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.3">Isa 41:3</reference>, and freq., with a personal obj. (<hi type="italic">eorum</hi>) <hi type="italic">quos non noveram,</hi> for the translation <hi type="italic">causam quam nesciebam</hi> (Jer.) gives a tame, almost meaningless, thought. With reference to the <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. in אחקרהוּ, on the form <hi type="italic">ehu</hi> used seldom by <hi type="italic">Waw consec.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.12.4">Job 12:4</reference>), and by the <hi type="italic">imper.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job 40:11</reference>), chiefly with a solemn calm tone of speech, vid., Ew. §250, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. Further: He spared not to render wrong-doers harmless, and snatched from them what they had taken from others. The cohortative form of the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.,</hi> ואשׁבּרה, has been discussed already on <reference osisRef="Job.1.15">Job 1:15</reference>; Job 19:20. The form מתלּעות is a transposition of מלתּעות, to render it more convenient for pronunciation, for the Arab. <hi type="italic">ṭl‛ , efferre se,</hi> whence a secondary form, Arab. <hi type="italic">tl‛ ,</hi> although used of the appearing of the teeth, furnishes no such appropriate primary signification as the Arab. <hi type="italic">lḏg , pungere, mordere,</hi> whence a secondary form, Arab. <hi type="italic">ltg ;</hi> the Aethiopic <hi type="italic">maltâht ,</hi> jawbone (<hi type="italic">maxilla</hi>), also favours מלתעה as the primary form. He shattered the grinders of the roguish, and by moral indignation against the robber he cast out of his teeth what he had stolen.
entries.c0b28dd0cbf988dab44254026bff537ea28483c7: <reference osisRef="Job.29.18-Job.20.18">Job 29:18-20 18</reference>  Then I thought: With my nest I shall expire, <div eID="gen8138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8139" type="x-p"/> And like the phoenix, have a long life. 19  My root will be open for water, <div eID="gen8139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8140" type="x-p"/> And the dew will lodge in my branches. 20  Mine honour will remain ever fresh to me, <div eID="gen8140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8141" type="x-p"/> And my bow will become young in my hand. <div eID="gen8141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8142" type="x-p"/> In itself, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.18">Job 29:18</reference></hi> might be translated: “and like to the sand I shall live many days” (Targ., Syr., Arab., Saad., Gecat., Luther, and, among moderns, Umbr., Stick., Vaih., Hahn, and others), so that the abundance of days is compared to the multitude of the grains of sand. The calculation of the immense total of grains of sand (atoms) in the world was, as is known, a favourite problem of antiquity; and in the Old Testament Scriptures, the comprehensive knowledge of Solomon is compared to “the sand upon the sea-shore,” 1Ki 5:9, - how much more readily a long life reduced to days! comp. Ovid, <hi type="italic">Metam</hi>. xiv. 136-138; <hi type="italic">quot haberet corpora pulvis, tot mihi natales contingere vana rogavi.</hi> We would willingly decide in favour of this rendering, which is admissible in itself, although a closer definition like היּם is wanting by כחול, if an extensive Jewish tradition did not secure the signification of an immortal bird, or rather one rising ever anew from the dead. The testimony is as follows: (1) <hi type="italic">b. Sanhedrin</hi> 108 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, according to which חול is only another name for the bird אורשׁינא,<note placement="foot">The name is a puzzle, and does not accord with any of the mythical birds mentioned in the Zendavesta (vid., Windischmann, <hi type="italic">Zoroastrische Studien,</hi> 1863, S. 93). What Lewysohn, <hi type="italic">Zoologie des Talmuds,</hi> S. 353, brings forward from the Greek by way of explanation is untenable. The name of the bird, <hi type="italic">Vâresha,</hi> in an obscure passage of the Bundehesch in Windischmann, <hi type="italic">ib.</hi> S. 80, is similar in sound. Probably, however, אורשׁינא is one and the same word as <hi type="italic">Simurg,</hi> which is composed of <hi type="italic">si</hi> (= <hi type="italic">sin</hi>) and <hi type="italic">murg</hi>, a bird (Pehlvi and Parsi <hi type="italic">mru</hi>). This <hi type="italic">si</hi> (<hi type="italic">sin</hi>) corresponds to the Vedic <hi type="italic">çjena</hi>, a falcon, and in the Zend form, <hi type="italic">çaêna</hi> (<hi type="italic">çîna</hi>), is the name of a miraculous bird; so that consequently <hi type="italic">Simurg</hi> = <hi type="italic">Sinmurg</hi>, Parsi <hi type="italic">Cînamru</hi>, signifies the <hi type="italic">Si-</hi> or <hi type="italic">Cîna</hi>-bird (comp. Kuhn, <hi type="italic">Herabkunft des Feuers,</hi> 1859, S. 125). In אורשינא the two parts of the composition seem to be reversed, and אור to be corrupted from מור. Moreover, the <hi type="italic">Simurg</hi> is like the phoenix only in the length of its life; another mythological bird, <hi type="italic">Kuknus</hi>, on the other hand (vid., the art. <hi type="italic">Phönix</hi> in Ersch u. Gruber), resembles it also in rising out of its own ashes.</note> of which the fable is there recorded, that when Noah fed the beasts in the ark, it sat quite still in its compartment, that it might not give more trouble to the patriarch, who had otherwise plenty to do, and that Noah wished it on this account the reward of immortality (יהא רעוא דלא תמות).   (2) That this bird חול is none other than the phoenix, is put beyond all doubt by the Midrashim (collected in the <hi type="italic">Jalkut</hi> on Job, §517). There it is said that Eve gave all the beasts to eat of the fruit of the forbidden tree, and that only one bird, the חול by name, avoided this death-food: “it lives a thousand years, at the expiration of which time fire springs up in its nest, and burns it up to about the size of an egg;” or even: that of itself it diminishes to that size, from which it then grows up again and continues to live (וחוזר ומתגדל איברים וחיה).   (3) The Masora observes, that כחול occurs in two different significations (בתרי לישׁני), since in the present passage it does not, as elsewhere, signify sand. (4) Kimchi, in his <hi type="italic">Lex.,</hi> says: “in a correct Jerusalem MS I found the observation: בשׁורק לנהרדעי ובחלם למערבאי, i.e., וכחוּל according to the Nehardean (Babylonian) reading, וכחול according to the western (Palestine) reading;” according to which, therefore, the Babylonian Masoretic school distinguished וכחול in the present passage from וכחול, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen 22:17</reference>, even in the pronunciation. A conclusion respecting the great antiquity of this lexical tradition may be drawn (5) from the lxx, which translates ὥσπερ στέλεχος φοίνικος, whence the Italic <hi type="italic">sicut arbor palmae,</hi> Jerome <hi type="italic">sicut palma</hi>. <div eID="gen8142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8143" type="x-p"/> If we did not know from the testimonies quoted that חול is the name of the phoenix, one might suppose that the lxx has explained וכחול according to the Arab. <hi type="italic">nachl ,</hi> the palm, as Schultens does; but by a comparison of those testimonies, it is more probable that the translation was ὥσπερ φοῖνιξ originally, and that ὥσπερ στέλεχος φοίνικος is an interpolation, for φοῖνιξ signifies both the immortal miraculous bird and the inexhaustibly youthful palm.<note placement="foot">According to Ovid, <hi type="italic">Metam</hi>. xv. 396, the phoenix makes its nest in the palm, and according to Pliny, <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> xiii. 42, it has its name from the palm: <hi type="italic">Phoenix putatur ex hujus palmae argumento nomen accepisse, iterum mori ac renasci ex se ipsa;</hi> vid., A. Hahmann, <hi type="italic">Die Dattelpalme, ihre Namen und ihre Verehrung in der alten Welt,</hi> in the periodical <hi type="italic">Bonplandia,</hi> 1859, Nr. 15, 16. Masius, in his studies of nature, has very beautifully described on what ground “the intelligent Greek gave a like name to the fabulous immortal bird that rises again out of its own ashes, and the palm which ever renews its youth.” Also comp. (Heimsdörfer’s) <hi type="italic">Christliche Kunstsymbolik,</hi> S. 26, and Augusti, <hi type="italic">Beiträge zur christl. Kunst-Geschichte und Liturgik,</hi> Bd. i. S. 106-108, but especially Piper, <hi type="italic">Mythologie der christl. Kunst</hi> (1847), i. 446f.</note> <div eID="gen8143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8144" type="x-p"/> We have the reverse case in Tertullian, <hi type="italic">de resurrectione carnis,</hi> c. xiii., which explains the passage in Ps; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.13">Psa 92:13</reference>, δίκαιος ὡς φοῖνιξ ἀντηήσει, according to the translation <hi type="italic">justus velut phoenix florebit,</hi> of the <hi type="italic">ales orientis </hi>or <hi type="italic">avis Arabiae,</hi> which symbolizes man’s immortality.<note placement="foot">Not without reference to Clemens Romanus, in his <hi type="italic">I. Ep. ad Corinth.</hi> c. xxv., according to which the phoenix is an Arabian bird, which lives five hundred years, then dies in a nest which it builds of incense, myrrh, and spices, and leaves behind it the larva of a young bird, which, when grown up, brings the nest with the bones of its father and places it upon the altar of the sun at the Egyptian Heliopolis. The source of this is Herodotus ii. 73) who, however, has an egg of myrrh instead of a nest of myrrh); and Tacitus, <hi type="italic">Ann</hi>. vi. 28, gives a similar narrative. Lactantius gives a different version in his poem on the phoenix, according to which this, the only one of its race, “built its nest in a country that remained untouched by the deluge.” The Jewish tragedy writer, Ezekiêlos, agrees more nearly with the statement of Arabia being the home of the phoenix. In his drama Ἐξαγωγή, a spy sent forward before the pilgrim band of Israel, he states that among other things the phoenix was also seen; vid., my <hi type="italic">Gesch. der jüd. Poesie,</hi> S. 219.</note> <div eID="gen8144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8145" type="x-p"/> Both figures, that of the phoenix and that of the palm, are equally appropriate and pleasing in the mouth of Job; but apart from the fact that the palm everywhere, where it otherwise occurs, is called תּמר, this would be the only passage where it occurs in the book of Job, which, in spite of its richness in figures taken from plants, nowhere mentions the palm, - a fact which is perhaps not accidental.<note placement="foot">Without attempting thereby to explain the phenomenon observed above, we nevertheless regard it as worthy of remark, that in general the palm is not a common tree either in Syria or in Palestine. “At present there are not in all Syria five hundred palm-trees; and even in the olden times there was no quantity of palms, except in the valley of the Jordan, and on the sea-coast.” - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8146" type="x-p"/> On the contrary, we must immediately welcome a reference to the Arabico-Egyptian myth of the phoenix, that can be proved, in a book which also otherwise thoroughly blends things Egyptian with Arabian, and the more so since (6) even the Egyptian language itself supports חול or חוּל as a name of the phoenix; for ΑΛΛΩΗ ΑΛΛΟΗ is explained in the Coptico-Arabic glossaries by <hi type="italic">es - semendel</hi> (the Arab. name of the phoenix, or at least a phoenix-like bird, that, like the salamander, <hi type="italic">semendar, </hi>cannot be burned), and in Kircher by <hi type="italic">avis Indica, species Phoenicis.</hi><note placement="foot">Vid., G. Seyffarth, <hi type="italic">Die Phoenix-Periode, Deutsche Morgenländ. Zeitschr.</hi> iii. (1849) 63ff., according to which <hi type="italic">alloê</hi> (Hierogl. <hi type="italic">koli</hi>) is the name of the false phoenix without head-feathers; <hi type="italic">bêne</hi> or <hi type="italic">bêni</hi> (Hierogl. bnno) is the name of the true phoenix with head-feathers, and the name of the palm also. <hi type="italic">Alloê</hi>, which accords with חול, is quite secured as a name of the phoenix.</note> חול is Hebraized from this Egyptian name of the phoenix; the word signifies rotation (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">haul</hi>, the year; <hi type="italic">haula</hi>, round about), and is a suitable designation of the bird that renews its youth periodically after many centuries of life: <hi type="italic">quae reparat seque ipsa reseminat ales</hi> (Ovid), not merely beginning a new life, but also bringing in a new great year: <hi type="italic">conversionem anni magni</hi> (Pliny); in the hieroglyphic representations it has the circle of the sun as a crown. In the full enjoyment of the divine favour and blessing, and in the consciousness of having made a right use of his prosperity, Job hoped φοίνικος ἔτη βιοῦν (Lucian, <hi type="italic">Hermot</hi>. 53), to use a Greek expression, and to expire or die עם־קנּי, as the first half of the verse, now brought into the right light, says. Looking to the form of the myth, according to which Ovid sings:<hi type="italic">Quassa cum fulvâ substravit cinnama myrrhâ, Se super imponit finitque in odoribus aevum,</hi> it might be translated: together with my nest (Umbr., Hirz., Hlgst.); but with the wish that he may not see any of his dear ones die before himself, there is at the same time connected the wish, that none of them should survive him, which is in itself unnatural, and diametrically opposed to the character of an Arab, who in the presence of death cherishes the twofold wish, that he may continue to live in his children (a proverb says: <hi type="italic">men chalaf el - weled el - fâlih ma mât ,</hi> he who leaves a noble child behind him is not dead), and that he may die in the midst of his family. Expressly this latter wish, עם־קני signifies: with = in my nest, i.e., in the bosom of my family, not without reference to the phoenix, which, according to the form of the myth in Herodotus, Pliny, Clemens, and others, brings the remains of its father in a nest or egg of myrrh to Heliopolis, into the sacred precincts of the temple of the sun, and thus pays him the last and highest tribute of respect. A different but similar version if given in Horapollo ii. 57, according to which the young bird came forth from the blood of its sire, σὺν τῷ πατρὶ πορεύεται εἰς τῆν Ἡλίου πόλιν τῆν ἐν Αιγύπτῳ, ὃς καὶ παραγενόμενος ἐκεῖ ἅμα τῇ ἡλίου ἀνατολῇ τελευτᾷ. The father, therefore, in death receives the highest tribute of filial respect; and it is this to which the hope of being able to die with (in) his nest, expressed by Job, refers. <div eID="gen8146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8147" type="x-p"/> The following substantival clause, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.19">Job 29:19</reference></hi>, is to be understood as future, like the similar clause, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.16">Job 29:16</reference></hi>, as perfect: my root - so I hoped - will remain open (unclosed) towards the water, i.e., it will never be deficient of water in its vicinity, that it may plentifully supply the stem and branches with nourishment, and dew will lodge on my branches, i.e., will descend nightly, and remain upon them to nourish them. אלי (corresponding to the Arab. <hi type="italic">ila ,</hi> originally <hi type="italic">ilai</hi>) occurs only in the book of Job, and here for the fourth and last time (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.3.22">Job 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.22">Job 15:22</reference>). קציר does not signify harvest here, as the ancient expositors render it, but, like <reference osisRef="Job.14.9">Job 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.16">Job 18:16</reference>, a branch, or the intertwined branches. The figure of the root and branch, the flow of vitality downwards and upwards, is the counterpart of Job 18:16. In <reference osisRef="Job.29.20">Job 29:20</reference> a substantival clause also comes first, as in <reference osisRef="Job.29.19">Job 29:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.16">Job 29:16</reference> (for the established reading is חדשׁ, not חדשׁ), and a verbal clause follows: his honour - so he hoped - should continue fresh by him, i.e., should abide with him in undiminished value and splendour. It is his honour before God and men that is intended, not his soul (Hahn); כבוד, δόξα, certainly is an appellation of the נפשׁ (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 98), but חדשׁ is not appropriate to it as predicate. By the side of honour stands manliness, or the capability of self-defence, whose symbol is the bow: and my bow should become young again in my hand, i.e., gain ever new strength and elasticity. It is unnecessary to supply כּח (Hirz., Schlottm., and others). The verb חלף, Arab. <hi type="italic">chlf</hi>, signifies, as the Arab. shows, properly to turn the back, then to go forth, exchange; the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. to make progress, to cause something new to come into the place of the old, to grow young again. These hopes introduced with ואמר were themselves an element of his former happiness. Its description can therefore be continued in connection with the ואמר without any fresh indication.
entries.aa01ef7cd134661d1aee1bf177728923b8e269c4: Job 29:21-25 21  They hearkened to me and waited, <div eID="gen8147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8148" type="x-p"/> And remained silent at my decision. 22  After my utterance they spake not again, <div eID="gen8148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8149" type="x-p"/> And my speech distilled upon them. 23  And they waited for me as for the rain, <div eID="gen8149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8150" type="x-p"/> And they opened their mouth wide for the latter rain. 24  I smiled to them in their hopelessness, <div eID="gen8150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8151" type="x-p"/> And the light of my countenance they cast not down. 25  I chose the way for them, and sat as chief, <div eID="gen8151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8152" type="x-p"/> And dwelt as a king in the army, <div eID="gen8152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8153" type="x-p"/> As one that comforteth the mourners. <div eID="gen8153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8154" type="x-p"/> Attentive, patient, and ready to be instructed, they hearkened to him (this is the force of שׁמע ל), and waited, without interrupting, for what he should say. ויחלּוּ, the pausal pronunciation with a reduplication of the last radical, as Jdg 5:7, חדלּוּ (according to correct texts), Ges. §20, 2, <hi type="italic">c;</hi> the reading of Kimchi, ויחלוּ, is the reading of Ben-Naphtali, the former the reading of Ben-Ascher (vid., Norzi). If he gave counsel, they waited in strictest silence: this is the meaning of ידּמוּ (<hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> of דּמם); למו, poetic for ל, refers the silence to its outward cause (vid., on <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">Hab 3:16</reference>). After his words <hi type="italic">non iterabant,</hi> i.e., as Jerome explanatorily translates: <hi type="italic">addere nihil audebant,</hi> and his speech came down upon them relieving, rejoicing, and enlivening them. The figure indicated in תּטּף is expanded in <reference osisRef="Job.29.23">Job 29:23</reference> after <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">Deu 32:2</reference> : they waited on his word, which penetrated deeply, even to the heart, as for rain, מטר, by which, as <reference osisRef="Job.29.23">Job 29:23</reference>, the so-called (autumnal) early rain which moistens the seed is prominently thought of. They open their mouth for the late rain, מלקושׁ (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.24.6">Job 24:6</reference>), i.e., they thirsted after his words, which were like the March or April rain, which helps to bring to maturity the corn that is soon to be reaped; this rain frequently fails, and is therefore the more longed for. פּער פּה is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Ps.119.131">Psa 119:131</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.81.11">Psa 81:11</reference>; and one must consider, in connection with it, what raptures the beginning of the periodical rains produces everywhere, where, as e.g., in Jerusalem, the people have been obliged for some time to content themselves with cisterns that are almost dried to a marsh, and how the old and young dance for joy at their arrival! <div eID="gen8154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8155" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference></hi> a thought as suited to the syntax as to the fact is gained if we translate: “I smiled to them - they believed it not,” i.e., they considered such condescension as scarcely possible (Saad., Raschi, Rosenm., De Wette, Schlottm., and others); עשׂחק is then <hi type="italic">fut. hypotheticum,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.10.16">Job 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job 20:24</reference>; Job 22:27., Ew. §357, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. But it does not succeed in putting <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference></hi> in a consistent relation to this thought; for, with Aben-Ezra, to explain: they did not esteem my favour the less on that account, my respect suffered thereby no loss among them, is not possible in connection with the biblical idea of “the light of the countenance;” and with Schlottm. to explain: they let not the light of my countenance, i.e., token of my favour, fall away, i.e., be in vain, is contrary to the usage of the language, according to which הפּיל פּנים signifies: to cause the countenance to sink (gloomily, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.5">Gen 4:5</reference>), whether one’s own, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jer 3:12</reference>, or that of another. Instead of פּני we have a more pictorial and poetical expression here, אור פּני: light of my countenance, i.e., my cheerfulness (as <reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Pro 16:15</reference>). Moreover, the אשׂחק אליהם, therefore, furnishes the thought that he laughed, and did not allow anything to dispossess him of his easy and contented disposition. Thus, therefore, those to whom Job laughed are to be thought of as in a condition and mood which his cheerfulness might easily sadden, but still did not sadden; and this their condition is described by לא יאמינוּ (a various reading in Codd. and editions is ולא), a phrase which occurred before (<reference osisRef="Job.24.22">Job 24:22</reference>) in the signification of being without faith or hope, despairing (comp. האמין, to gain faith, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference>), - a clause which is not to be taken as attributive (Umbr., Vaih.: who had not confidence), but as a neutral or circumstantial subordinate clause (Ew. §341, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). Therefore translate: I smiled to them, if they believed not, i.e., despaired; and however despondent their position appeared, the cheerfulness of my countenance they could not cause to pass away. However gloomy they were, they could not make me gloomy and off my guard. Thus also <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.29.25">Job 29:25</reference></hi> is now suitably attached to the preceding: I chose their way, i.e., I made the way plain, which they should take in order to get out of their hopeless and miserable state, and sat as chief, as a king who is surrounded by an armed host as a defence and as a guard of honour, attentive to the motion of his eye; not, however, as a sovereign ruler, but as one who condescended to the mourners, and comforted them (נחם <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, properly to cause to breathe freely). This peaceful figure of a king brings to mind the warlike one, Job 15:24. כּאשׁר is not a conj. here, but equivalent to כאישׁ אשׁר, <hi type="italic">ut</hi> (<hi type="italic">quis</hi>) <hi type="italic">qui;</hi> consequently not: as one comforts, but: as he who comforts; lxx correctly: ὃν τρόπον παθεινοὺς παρακαλῶν. The accentuation (כאשׁר <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>, אבלים <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, ינחם <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>) is erroneous; כאשׁר should be marked with <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch,</hi> and אבלים with <hi type="italic">Mercha-Zinnorith.</hi> <div eID="gen8155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8156" type="x-p"/> From the prosperous and happy past, absolutely passed, Job now turns to the present, which contrasts so harshly with it.  <chapter eID="Job.29"/> <div eID="gen8156" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="21">21.                   <ns0:p n="22">22.                   <ns0:p n="23">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:410" />23. And they waited for me, as for the rain <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">As the Earth or the Husbandman waiteth <ns0:hi>for the rain,</ns0:hi> to wit, the former rain<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of which see <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 11. 14. because <ns0:hi>the latter rain</ns0:hi> is here opposed to it: See <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 5. 7.</ns0:note>, and they opened their mouth <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To receive my words, and therewith to satisfie their thirst, as the dry and parched Earth gapes or opens its mouth to receive the Rain.</ns0:note> for me <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> for the lat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter rain.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. <ns0:hi>If</ns0:hi> I laughed on them <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>sported,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>jested with them i. e.</ns0:hi> carried my self familiarly and pleasantly with them.</ns0:note>, they believed <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">It was so acceptable to them to see me well-pleased with them, that they could scarce believe their Eyes and Ears that it was so: Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 45. 26. <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 126. 1.</ns0:note>, and the light of my countenance they cast not down <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">My familiarity did not breed contempt or presump<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion in them to say or do any thing that might grieve me, or make my countenance to fall, as it doth in case of shame or sorrow, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4. 5. They were very cautious not to abuse my smiles, nor to give me any occasion to change my Countenance or carriage to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25. And no less acceptable was my presence to them.</ns0:note>, as one <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> comforteth the mourners <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">As I was able and ready to comfort any afflicted or sorrowful persons, so my Consolations were always grateful and welcom to them.
